title: Lior and the Summer
premise: August Delacroix, a cellist whose career shattered on stage twelve years ago, has built a careful life around a failing bakery and a rule: never be seen wanting anything. When his sister begs him to bring a date to the Delacroix family reunion, he hires Lior Vance, a charming stranger who turns out to be the estranged heir of the very family that once owned August's grandmother. As their fake romance deepens into something real, August must confront the family that broke him, Lior must choose between reclaiming his inheritance and dismantling it, and both must decide whether love is worth the risk of being truly known. It ends with August performing again—small, unafraid—while Lior signs away his claim to the family fortune, choosing instead a lease renewal, a shared apartment above the bakery, and a life measured in brave steps together.
about_author: Ines Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former orchestral librarian who spent a decade backstage before turning to fiction about people who perform for their lives. She writes from a drafty coastal house where the bakery downstairs never quite closes.

chapters.title: The Last Train Rule
chapters.summary: August's POV. We meet him closing the bakery at exactly nine, counting safe routines like rosary beads, until his sister Margot calls with an ultimatum: bring a date to the reunion or face the family alone. Emotional beat: the ache of a life built too small.

chapters.title: A Stranger Who Smiles Like Weather
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior, newly arrived in town and sleeping in his car by choice rather than poverty, overhears August arguing with Margot and offers himself as a fake date—for gas money and a reason to stay. Beat: two lonely people recognizing each other's camouflage.

chapters.title: Terms and Conditions
chapters.summary: August's POV. They negotiate rules over burnt croissants: no real names' histories, no touching after dessert, no one stays past the last train. Lior breaks rule three within hours by falling asleep in the bakery chair. Beat: reluctant tenderness.

chapters.title: Twelve Years Ago
chapters.summary: Flashback through August's POV. The catastrophic final performance: frozen mid-cadenza, heckled, filmed, memed, abandoned by his mentor father who called it 'a waste of tuition.' Beat: understanding why invisibility became survival.

chapters.title: The Delacroix Name
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Researching August online, Lior discovers the viral video—and realizes his own family, the Vances, once employed August's grandmother as a housekeeper before evicting her. He says nothing. Beat: guilt as a held breath.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: August's POV. A practice run of couplehood: shared stories, invented anniversary, hands almost touching over flour-dusted counters. Lior plays piano badly; August almost laughs for the first time in months. Beat: joy sneaking past the guards.

chapters.title: Margot Sees Everything
chapters.summary: Margot's POV. Margot clocks the way August looks at Lior and privately grieves, knowing what their parents did to anyone August loved. She warns Lior obliquely: 'He doesn't break. He just stops.' Beat: protective dread.

chapters.title: The Reunion, Act One
chapters.summary: August's POV. Arrival at the family estate: marble, judgment, his father's appraising handshake. Lior performs charm flawlessly while August white-knuckles a wine glass. Beat: terror wearing a borrowed suit.

chapters.title: The Reunion, Act Two
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Dessert arrives and the performance stops feeling fake—Lior defends August against a backhanded toast about 'the cellist,' shocking the table. August's hand finds his under the linen. Beat: the fake becomes real by dessert, exactly as feared.

chapters.title: Missed Trains
chapters.summary: August's POV. They miss the last train home deliberately. On the estate's dark lawn, almost-kiss interrupted by August's panic attack. Lior holds him without questions. Beat: intimacy arriving sideways, through crisis.

chapters.title: Bakery Hours
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Morning after: Lior learns the bakery's lease expires in six weeks and the landlord is a Vance subsidiary. He quietly begins pulling strings he swore not to pull. Beat: help curdling into control.

chapters.title: The Grandmother's Letters
chapters.summary: August's POV. August shows Lior letters his grandmother wrote from service in the Vance house—warm toward young Lior's late mother, bitter toward the patriarch. Lior goes pale. Beat: history pressing its thumb on the present.

chapters.title: First Kiss, Bad Timing
chapters.summary: Dual POV. A rainstorm, a closed sign, a kiss that tastes like admission—interrupted by a call from the Vance estate inviting Lior (recognized now as the missing heir) to dinner. Beat: happiness interrupted by inheritance.

chapters.title: The Heir Apparent
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior confesses everything: the name, the money, the eviction. August feels the floor tilt—the man he kissed owns the paper on his bakery. Beat: betrayal discovered before it was committed.

chapters.title: Closed for Inventory
chapters.summary: August's POV. Three days of silence. August bakes compulsively, cataloguing every moment that might have been manipulation. Margot forces him to admit he's in love, which makes it worse. Beat: grief rehearsing itself early.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior meets his uncle, who dangles full reinstatement if he'll sever ties with 'that baker boy' and let the lease lapse—a test of loyalty dressed as opportunity. Beat: power showing its teeth.

chapters.title: Counteroffer
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Instead, Lior secretly uses his leverage to freeze the eviction proceedings, buying August time without telling him. First corruption of good intentions. Beat: protection becoming patronage.

chapters.title: Reconciliation, Uneven Terms
chapters.summary: August's POV. They reconcile—but August doesn't know about the lease maneuver, and Lior lets the silence stand. The kiss again, sweeter now, built on a hairline crack. Beat: love with an asterisk.

chapters.title: Cello in the Back Room
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior finds August's cello, still in its case, and asks him to play. August refuses, then plays eight bars at midnight, shaking. Lior understands the wound is not the failure but the father. Beat: witness as intimacy.

chapters.title: Family Dinner, Round Two
chapters.summary: August's POV. Dinner at the Vance estate as Lior's guest. August sees the machine of wealth up close and watches Lior get absorbed, charmed, claimed. He leaves early. Beat: jealousy of a world, not a person.

chapters.title: The Uncle's Gambit
chapters.summary: Villain-adjacent POV via Lior. The uncle leaks to August that Lior 'bought' his lease extension—framing rescue as ownership. Beat: poison delivered as truth.

chapters.title: What Money Can't Say
chapters.summary: August's POV. Confrontation: 'You didn't save me, you acquired me.' Lior can't explain without admitting he defied his uncle, so he says nothing useful. August walks. Beat: the exact shape of miscommunication.

chapters.title: Empty Chair, Full Ovens
chapters.summary: August's POV. Weeks pass. August throws himself into the bakery's final stretch, deciding to close gracefully rather than fight. Margot stages an intervention involving every regular customer. Beat: community as found family.

chapters.title: The Regulars
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, rotating micro-POVs. The bakery's cast—retired teacher, night nurse, teenage poet—organize a lease-buying cooperative. August resists charity; Margot reframes it as investment. Beat: he is not invisible; he never was.

chapters.title: Lior Alone
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior formally renounces his claim at a board meeting, burning his bridge in a cold, precise speech. His uncle retaliates: the lease freeze reverses, eviction accelerates. Beat: sacrifice with immediate cost.

chapters.title: News Travels
chapters.summary: August's POV. August learns secondhand that Lior gave up everything—and that the eviction is now worse because of it. Guilt and fury tangle. Beat: love as liability.

chapters.title: The Letter He Never Sent
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior writes a letter explaining everything and doesn't send it, instead leaving it with Margot 'in case.' He takes work playing piano in a hotel bar, humbled. Beat: pride finally set down.

chapters.title: Father's Verdict
chapters.summary: August's POV. August's father appears at the bakery, offering to fund it—if August publicly retires from music forever, calling the cello 'settled business.' Beat: the original wound offered a bandage made of salt.

chapters.title: No Thanks
chapters.summary: August's POV. August refuses his father for the first time in his life, out loud, in front of customers. Hands steady. Something unlocks. Beat: the first brave step measured large.

chapters.title: Reading the Letter
chapters.summary: August's POV. Margot surrenders Lior's letter. August reads it twice, weeping into proofing dough, understanding at last that Lior's silences were fear, not contempt. Beat: forgiveness beginning as comprehension.

chapters.title: Finding Him at the Bar
chapters.summary: August's POV. August finds Lior playing half-empty hotel lounges, sits through three sets, then requests a song only they share—their fake anniversary song. Beat: pursuit reversed, hope re-lit.

chapters.title: Terms and Conditions, Revised
chapters.summary: Dual POV. New rules: no secrets, no rescues without asking, last train abolished. They rebuild slowly, honestly, over inventory spreadsheets and sheet music. Beat: love renegotiated as partnership.

chapters.title: Eviction Notice
chapters.summary: August's POV. The formal eviction notice arrives—thirty days. But this time August doesn't fold. He calls the cooperative, calls Margot, calls a lawyer who used to buy sourdough. Beat: fear met with infrastructure.

chapters.title: The Board Meeting Crash
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior returns to the Vance board one final time—not as heir but as whistleblower, exposing the uncle's predatory leasing scheme targeting small businesses citywide. Beat: power turned against corruption.

chapters.title: Public Record
chapters.summary: August's POV. The scandal breaks; the lease scheme collapses; the bakery's building transfers to a community trust. Reporters ask August about the viral cellist video. He answers, calmly, on record. Beat: the past renamed.

chapters.title: One Song, One Night
chapters.summary: August's POV. The bakery hosts a fundraiser concert. August plays a full piece for the first time in twelve years—imperfect, alive, Lior's eyes on him the whole way. Beat: climax of identity; the stage reclaimed.

chapters.title: The Father Comes to Listen
chapters.summary: August's POV. His father attends the encore, waiting afterward to critique. August thanks him for coming and means nothing by it—finally free of needing the verdict. Beat: the wound closes from the inside.

chapters.title: Lease Renewal
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior signs the new lease as a co-signer, his name beside August's, first document he's ever signed with joy. Keys exchanged; boxes moved upstairs. Beat: domesticity as victory.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: August's POV. Quiet epilogue-feel chapter: morning routine, two coffee mugs, Lior teaching himself bread, August teaching Lior cello scales badly. No trains to catch. Beat: safety redefined as chosen, not small.

chapters.title: Summer, Extended
chapters.summary: Dual POV, final. One year later: the bakery thrives, the cooperative houses three more businesses, and August books a small honest recital. Last line mirrors the first—he locks up at nine, but leaves the light on for someone staying. Beat: completion; love as a door left open.
